summary: St. Johns River Light at Mayport: a light from 1830 and a brick tower first lit in 1859, now inside Naval Station Mayport; the light ended in 1929 or 1931.

structures.note: Present height 81 ft per the nomination; LighthouseFriends gives 74 ft as built and says the 1887 raising was not made. Unresolved.

access.note: Inside Naval Station Mayport; base access limited since 9/11; visible from Palmer Street through a chain-link fence (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Grounds open by permission of the Navy; tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: First tower built near the river mouth (LighthouseFriends; $10,500 expended in 1830, nomination).
First tower undermined by the sea and torn down; second tower built roughly a mile inland.
Brick tower, the third on the site, first exhibited 1 January 1859.
Light shot out during the Civil War; LighthouseFriends dates it 1864 and says some attributed it to John Daniels. The nomination's text dates the extinguishing to 1867 (OCR). Disputed.
Given a new third-order lens and lantern and relit on 4 July 1867 (LighthouseFriends).
Nomination: tower raised fifteen feet to present height. LighthouseFriends: the Board's proposed raising was not carried out. Disputed.
Thermostat installed to warn of a broken mantle; experiments reported in the Bulletin.
Lamp overheated and caught fire; keeper Amos Buford put it out and relit it (Bulletin 1915; LighthouseFriends).
Semiautomatic radiobeacon placed in operation; the Bulletin calls it the first of its type in the United States.
Nomination: abandoned 15 January 1929, replaced by a lightship. LighthouseFriends: a few months more, then discontinued 5 May 1931. Disputed.
Discontinued 5 May 1931 (LighthouseFriends); the roster's last head keeper is listed to 1931.
In the 1940s fill from Ribault Bay was brought in for the naval runway, burying the original door (LighthouseFriends; year approximate).
Rehabilitation honoured by a preservation award from the City of Jacksonville and the Jacksonville Historic Landmarks Commission (plaque, per LighthouseFriends).
Naval base closed to the public after 9/11 (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.proposed: Remove from us-fl-st-johns-river; the record belongs to us-fl-st-johns (Saint Johns Light, 1954)
corrections.why: NPGallery's record for 100002224 is titled 'Saint Johns Light', period 1954-1967 (architects: USCG, Skinner, James H. Small Construction Co.). It is the 1954 successor light, not the 1859 brick tower. The asset page as read gives no location.
The brick tower was first exhibited on 1 January 1859 (LighthouseFriends; nomination 'completed January 1'). 1858 is the start of work in the winter of 1857-58 (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends says work on the brick tower began in the winter of 1857-58 and that it was first exhibited on 1 January 1859. The 1858 entry in the record looks like the start of work, so the first light is 1859 (see corrections).

Nomination: 81 ft present height after a fifteen-foot raising in 1887. LighthouseFriends: 74 ft as built, and the raising not carried out. The record's 25.0 m is between the two and is not settled by the sources.

notes_for_editor:
1. Roster match: the USLHS place is 'St. Johns River' (slug st-johns-river; Mayport, Duval County; established 1830; discontinued 1929), matched by name and county. The archive's coordinates for it are about 40 km from the record's, which the roster tool attributes to USLHS positions being to the minute. The 1954 'St. Johns' light (slug st-johns, roster 1959-64) is a different station and is not used here.
2. Discontinuance: the nomination gives abandonment on 15 January 1929; LighthouseFriends gives discontinuance on 5 May 1931 after a few months with the lightship on station; the roster runs to 1931. The record's deactivated 1929 is kept; both dates appear in events. The editor should decide.
3. Civil War: LighthouseFriends dates the shooting-out to 1864 with relighting on 4 July 1867. The nomination's text reads 'Light was extinguished in 1867 by Rebels' in a passage about the war; the year may be an OCR error or a real difference. A Lighthouse Board report for 1864-67 is not in the corpus.
4. Tower height and the 1887 raising: nomination 81 ft and a fifteen-foot raising; LighthouseFriends 74 ft and the raising not made. Unresolved.
5. 1889 proposal: the nomination places it on Fort George Island; the Board's 1891 report and LighthouseFriends place it on Mount Cornelia (north side of the river, 62 ft above sea level). Both are reported in the story.
6. OCR: the nomination's '1859' appears as 'U 59' in the OCR; read as 1859 and matched by LighthouseFriends. The nomination's '1853' appears as '3353' and is not used. The 1891 Board quotation is OCR-damaged; the quoted fragment is clean.
7. Keepers: all 24 USLHS roster lines are included with their archive person slugs. Two roster names appear in two roles (Augustus W. Brown; Josephine Daniels appears in two stints). Frances McDonald is not linked to Alexander McDonald; no inference.
8. NRHP 100002224 is 'Saint Johns Light' (1954-1967), the successor light, and is removed from this station in corrections; the story mentions it as a separate light.
9. NRHP listing year: the record gives 1976 from the reference number 76002237; the plaque LighthouseFriends describes says 1982. Not changed.
10. Newspapers: a Chronicling America search for 'Mayport' with 'lighthouse' in Florida papers, 1929-1931, returned no hits. No other newspaper search was run for this station.
11. The 1912 candlepower increase and the 1886-era records in the nomination's OCR are not used.
12. Disagreement stated in the story: the 1834 rebuilding appropriation is $10,500 in the nomination and $10,550 on 30 June 1834 in LighthouseFriends. Both are given.
13. Keeper name spelling: LighthouseFriends prints Matthew H. Phillips; the roster and the story use Philips.
14. Focal height: no source read gives a focal height, so the earlier 77 ft / 23.5 m was removed from facts. The lens 'removed' status was also unsupported and was removed.
15. The grounds are open by permission of the Navy (LighthouseFriends), so visit.grounds_open is true; the earlier false value contradicted the source.
16. Charleston earthquake (31 August 1886) felt at the station: LighthouseFriends prints Augustus Brown's report. The 1891 'complaints' passage is on scan page 461 of the 1891 report; the 1893 report repeats it on scan page 140.
17. The 1915 Buford report (dated 4 May 1915) is in the Bulletin on PDF page 26 (printed page 171, under the heading 'Alarm bells at light stations'); the 1914 thermostat paragraph is on PDF page 10.
18. The NPGallery asset page read here gives no location for Saint Johns Light; the story no longer places it on the naval station.
